title: Nada
hookLine: John of the Cross: nothing, nothing, nothing, and on the mountain, nothing: letting go for love
last: THE KING IS IN THE CENTER.

cards: A small sketch of a mountain, drawn by hand. At the bottom, paths split off. On the wrong roads, the drawing is labeled with the things people chase: having, knowing, comfort, glory.
Up the narrow middle path, one word repeats, again and again, and near the top of the mountain, the same word once more. Nada. Nothing.
The sketch was made by a Spanish Carmelite friar, Teresa's companion in reforming their order, known as John of the Cross; you met his dark night on day two hundred seventy-seven.
And nada sounds, at first, like a bleak word to put on a mountain.

teach.h: NADA IS THE PRICE, TODO THE PRIZE.
teach.b: Here's what John means, and it isn't despair. In The Ascent of Mount Carmel, he gives short sayings that work like a riddle. To come to enjoy everything, desire to enjoy nothing.
To come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing. To come to know everything, desire to know nothing. Nada is the price, and todo, everything, is the prize.
The nothing is for the sake of the all. Why? A heart full of grasping has no room left.
If your hands are clenched around a pile of small things, you can't receive the one great thing.

teach.h: NOT HATRED OF THE WORLD, LOOSER GRIP.
teach.b: So the nothing isn't hatred of the world. Mountains, rivers, the night air: John's poems are full of them. The nothing is about the grip, letting go of the clutch, the need to own, so that love has space.
Paul says something close in his letter to the Philippians: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord."
Not that everything is worthless; next to the one thing, he can let the rest go. John isn't gentle about how hard this is. Letting go can feel like loss, like night.
Yet his mountain is drawn going up.

teach.h: THE PATH OF NOTHING GOES UP.
teach.b: The narrow path of nothing is the one that reaches the top, and near the summit, where the word is nada again, he places God's honor and glory. In John's picture, empty hands at the top turn out to be full.

how: Carmelites and others who follow John of the Cross practice detachment, letting go of attachments to things, comforts and even spiritual feelings, so that the heart is free to love God; it is often taught with a spiritual director.

o: the belief that life and the world are worthless
letting go of grasping, to make room for God's all
a vow of silence kept by Carmelite friars

games.q: the mountain of nada — tap the pairs.
p: I count all things but loss

s: for John, nada means the world is worthless
his poems are full of mountains and rivers. nada is about the grip, not hatred.
in John's sayings, the nothing is for the sake of the all
to come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing.
on John's sketch, the path of nothing leads down
it's the narrow middle path, and it goes up the mountain.

games.q: you're on John's mountain. three roads: one for having, one for knowing, one marked nada. which does he draw going to the top?
games.why: John labels the narrow middle path nada, and it's the one that climbs. emptied hands, in his picture, are the ones that can receive.

practice: Close one hand into a firm fist, feel the grip, and ask what you're gripping right now: an object, a plan, being right in an argument, an image of yourself.
Pick just one, and slowly, a finger at a time, not in disgust, let the fist uncurl and your hold on that one thing loosen with it.
If you pray, offer it to God as the hand opens; if you don't, just feel the difference between the grip and the release.

wordCard.voice: Nada. Spanish for nothing. In John of the Cross, the letting go that makes room for everything, for love.

orig.note: Greek: loss, damage; Paul's word in Philippians 3:8, I count all things but loss.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing, for all. A clenched hand can't receive. Rest well.
